To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

CD4 lymphopenia in patients with long-term virological control of HIV on HAART is associated with a skewed, senesced, and dysfunctional T cell phenotype, characterized by a reduced frequency of naive and HIV-specific T cells, an increased frequency of senesced and Th2-commited T cells, and an inefficient HIV-specific CD4 T cell function.

HIV-infected patients that fail to recover their CD4+ T cells despite virologically suppressed antiretroviral therapy (HAART) display an altered T-cell maturation, with a predominance of effector memory cells and a reduction of unprimed naïve cells.
HIV-infected patients on long-term suppressive HAART with low CD4 cell counts have a skewed, senesced T-cell maturation pattern and poor HIV-specific T-cell function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the immunology of the host immune response to the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.
the immunological consequences of CD4+ lymphopenia on virologially suppressive HAART, which is of clinical importance in the era of HAART.
the development of new therapeutic strategies to overcome T-cell dysfunction in INRs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV infection, in particular in INRs, is associated with an aberrant T-cell maturation pattern and function.
CD4 lymphopenia is a major factor in HIV disease progression.
CD4+ lymphopenia in the presence of virologically suppressed HAART is associated with an impaired immune reconstitution and a skewed maturation pattern in T cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIV-infected INR patients have a skewed T-cell differentiation profile, which is characterized by an increased proportion of effector memory T cells and reduced naive T cells in the periphery.

HIV-infected patients who fail to achieve CD4+ recovery despite long-term virological suppression on HAART have a skewed T-cell maturing profile with a predominance of effector memory and senescent T cells.

we show for the first time that the T cell phenotype of INRs is skewed towards senescent cells, which may contribute to the poor immune response to HIV and the poor clinical outcome in these patients.
